articles.title: #CourageON: Why this climate activist still believes in COP31
articles.summary: For Joshua Villalobos, COP31 would be a success if it means more money flowing into the communities he works with, particularly for projects that provide renewable energy

blocks.text: “Am I optimistic about this COP? Well, that’s a challenging question.”

Usually quick-witted, Joshua Villalobos took time to gather his thoughts about the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) happening this November. He is a climate activist and secretary-general of the Negrosanon Initiative for Climate and the Environment (NICE). In November 2025, we featured him in a story on young Filipinos championing renewable energy across the Philippines.
“Sometimes, the talks within the negotiations are taking so much time. The talks have been ongoing [for] the past three decades.”

The world has struggled to meet the commitments made in these negotiations. For one, countries agreed in 2015 to keep global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial temperatures, while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius.
“There’s a new report that we’ll overshoot the 1.5,” he said.

The work of climate activists like Joshua isn’t confined to the streets. Behind the placards and protests, they pore over lengthy documents and study climate policies. Joshua, in fact, finds the law “beautiful.” But what keeps him invested in the negotiations is the possibility of seeing solutions.
“Most of these solutions are being championed by communities, people’s organizations, environmental movements. These are things that I am optimistic about.”

blocks.caption: WORK. Members of NICE conduct a meeting at their hub in Bacolod City. Photo by Aidan Bernales/Rappler

blocks.text: Based in Bacolod City, Joshua works closely with the people of Matabas Island in Sagay City, Negros Occidental. Matabas, like many small islands in the Philippines, used to have no electricity.

Once, at night, Joshua witnessed island residents sleeping outside their homes. Without electricity, households didn’t have the luxury of electric fans or air-conditioning. “We are seeing how they are paying the price in their daily lives, sleeping outside because of the heat,” he said.

Through partnerships with foundations, Joshua’s organization, NICE, installed solar panels to light up communal areas, including the island’s walkways. NICE now hopes to power the island’s water desalination facility to give residents access to fresh water. It also plans to bring electricity to the island’s only school.
For Joshua, COP31 would be a success if it meant more money flowing into the communities he works with, particularly for projects that provide renewable energy.
During COP30 in 2025, parties agreed to develop a just transition mechanism. This year, discussions are expected to further define how the mechanism will work.

NICE is a member of Aksyon Klima Pilipinas, a Philippine civil society network that prepares policy positions and proposals ahead of COP. The network also held a pre-COP31 conference on just transition in October.
For Joshua, the pre-COP31 conference was an important opportunity to bring the realities of communities in Negros and other parts of the Philippines into the discussions.
“We know that these communities are already paying the price for the impacts of the climate crisis,” Joshua explained.
“If we don’t make the transition just, then they will most likely pay the price of the transition… through job displacement, land displacement, or environmental degradation.”

blocks.caption: MATABAS ISLAND. Joshua Villalobos (extreme left) visits Matabas Island in Sagay City, Negros Occidental, to work on the island’s solar-powered facilities in October 2026. Photo courtesy of Joshua Villalobos

blocks.text: Joshua will attend the second week of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, bringing with him stories from the communities he has worked with.
“It is exactly because of the work that we are doing year-round [that] we are going to the COP more informed about the realities of the communities and demand what the COP should deliver.”

Still, Joshua is not confident that the negotiations will deliver political breakthroughs. Climate negotiations tend to be exclusive, technical, and jargon-laden. Joshua understands why young people and communities affected by the climate crisis might lose faith in the process. Many of them also struggle to find the money to participate.

Asked why he continues to attend the annual climate conference despite its shortcomings, he answered: “For now, there’s no alternative for that kind of global space where communities can raise our voices and governments are there.”
“It is still a space that we must not give up on, and we should continue to fight for.” – Rappler.com

#CourageON is a bi-monthly newsletter providing updates from our communities. In time for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), the month of November features stories of courage and resilience from our partner communities and advocates.

articles.title: [Rear View] A ‘pink wave’ in 2028? Not so fast
articles.summary: The pink movement needs to accept that the ground shifted in 2016, a shift affirmed in 2019 and 2022. It cannot wait for history to repeat itself, and should not plan for it.

blocks.text: The day after the historic midterm elections in the United States, the Liberal Party (LP) and Akbayan, the organized core formations of the pink movement, released statements hailing the Democratic “blue wave.” Pink online pundits and the faithful boldly prophesied a “pink wave” in 2028, declaring that if it can happen in Donald Trump’s America, it can happen here.

The liberal progressive bloc’s affinity with the Democrats, the democratic socialist wing in particular, runs deep. They share the vocabulary and cultural anchors. They are evangelistic in their campaigns to fire up the youth vote. But the “blue wave” rode a national grievance over prices and an unpopular war. The pinks would do well to proceed with caution.

The 2028 election is not a midterm; it’s an open race for the presidency. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., thankfully, cannot run again, but he is very much a player in 2028 despite his absence from the ballot. The abysmal state of the economy, the high cost of living, soaring prices, inefficient public services, and corruption are his legacy, and that legacy gives voters the permission structure to support anybody but a Marcos clone.
The question, and the challenge, for the pinks is who collects the grievance vote. The surveys all say it’s Vice President Sara Duterte.

She remains the front-runner despite unexplained wealth allegations now at the center of her impeachment trial and persistent questions about her grasp of policy. Pulse Asia’s September survey had her at 50% nationally, nearly double Leni Robredo’s 26. In Mindanao, where identity politics comes into play, she is at 92%. Other surveys show support for her thinning, but she remains, for now, the candidate of the aggrieved.

Unless the Senate impeachment court convicts her and declares her unfit for public office, the Vice President is the competition for the anti-incumbent vote, and the pinks will have to capture those voters from her.

Unlike the two-party system, our multi-party system extends to voters a wide range of choices. In a crowded field, a fractured opposition in 2028 is a gift to the Vice President. Brazil and Serbia offer better models of coalition building than the US: progressive presidential candidates won by working with people and parties outside their own base, a concept that the pink movement has always found hard to embrace.

The pinks did have their “pink wave” moment in the 2025 midterms, with real and hard earned victories. But the presidency is a winner-take-all contest, and the same movement that can elect senators and party-lists can lose the presidency. We saw it in 2022: the pink movement mustered the largest rallies and the most star-studded endorsements in recent memory, and Robredo still finished with roughly 15 million votes to Marcos’s nearly 32 million.

With presidential voter turnout at above 80%, the pinks cannot win by just mobilizing their own. They have to persuade voters who voted for Marcos and Duterte in 2022, the same voters they continue to regard with disdain and talk down to.

The LP also carries a burden the US Democrats, for all their troubles, do not. For many voters, the LP has come to embody elitist politics. It is a damaged brand, and the damage is partly self-inflicted.

The Democrats did not win on decency. They won on affordability, and on high gas prices as a result of the Iran war, with strong candidates perfectly fitted for the states they ran in. The Liberals and their pink allies proudly declared itself “disente” in 2016 and 2019, and the DDS caricatured them as preachy, elitist, and out of touch.

Unfortunately, that caricature has taken hold, and it is an uncomfortable weakness they must confront. If they want to be relevant in 2028, talk less about character and more about gut issues, about bigas, kuryente, at trabaho.

The party’s old guards still wish for another 2010. The late Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino was an accidental candidate. His mother’s death in August 2009 put him front and center, Mar Roxas stepped aside, and a grieving nation found its standard-bearer in a matter of weeks, one who was the opposite of outgoing president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo.
It happened at a time when mainstream media still had the power to make or unmake candidates. That country no longer exists.

Voters today live in partisan chambers that are both political and identity-based. Partisans are willing to overlook the character flaws of politicians they regard as their own, and to disbelieve anything that comes from the other side. A sympathy wave needs a shared audience, and there is no shared audience anymore. The pinks cannot wait for history to repeat itself, and they should not plan for it.

Before the pink movement plunges into the murky, gritty battles of 2028, it needs to look inward, to accept that the ground shifted in 2016, a shift affirmed in 2019 and 2022. The liberal opposition failed, or refused, to recalibrate, bemoaning disinformation without confronting it head on, dismissing unfavorable surveys while extolling favorable ones, no matter how questionable the science. And it bears repeating: it must stop blaming the voters for their own shortcomings.
Finally, it must accept one inconvenient fact: Robredo, hailed as the movement’s face and hope, has said she will not run in 2028. Liberal stalwarts and ardent supporters, however, refuse to give up.

So go ahead and admire the Democrats, but use their victory as an opportunity for self-reflection. With neither a machinery nor, as of today, a candidate, the pinks are not yet primed to secure the votes of aggrieved Filipinos. The hard work began yesterday. – Rappler.com
Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.

articles.title: Trump says he was 'kidding' about Dana White press secretary offer
articles.summary: The president told the Ultimate Fighting Championship boss to "please take the job" in a Truth Social post on Saturday.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has said he "was kidding" about asking Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be the White House press secretary.
Trump told the media on Sunday that White "loves the idea" but that the invitation was "just a little fun".
It comes after the president posted on his Truth Social platform on Saturday that he had offered White the role, asking him to take it while writing, "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other."
White said later that day he was going to meet the president on Monday, but would not be drawn into whether or not he would take the vacant position.
On Sunday Trump told reporters White was visiting him on Monday for "other reasons".
"I think he's going to be in Washington. So he's going to come over and see me.
"I will tell you, I was only kidding. But Dana loves the idea. And there's only one Dana. He's great," the president said.
"But, it was it was just a little fun."
The press secretary role is yet to be filled after it became vacant in October when Katie Zacharia quit after less than five days in the job.
She took over from Karoline Leavitt, who was the youngest press secretary in US history and had held the role since Trump began his second term.
Trump's job offer came after a heavy loss in the midterm elections, where the Republican Party lost its majority in both houses of Congress.
In his Truth Social post on Saturday, he said he was "pleased to announce" that White "has been offered the job".
He said he had asked White to bring with him several current and former mixed martial arts fighters as "assistants".
"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," he wrote.
"Dana, please take the job!"
Asked about the Trump offer at a news conference on Saturday, the UFC chief executive said he had "lot of jobs already".
"I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that," he said of their planned Monday meeting, but did not say whether or not he would take the job.
White leads UFC, and PowerSlap , a regulated slap-fighting promotion league, as well as recently launching promotion company Zuffa Boxing.
He is also a board member of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
White appeared as a speaker in support of Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

articles.title: Turkey pushes for transition at COP31 as coal burns
articles.summary: The host of this year's UN climate summit remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels as it tries to inspire a global switch to clean energy.

image.caption: Solar energy capacity in Turkey has skyrocketed over the last decade, though coal power still dominates the gridImage: Emrah Gurel/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: As Turkey welcomes delegates to the 2026 UN climate talks in Antalya and pushes for cuts in global greenhouse gas emissions, it can point to surging renewable energy capacity at home.
The COP31 host has approved more than 33 gigawatts (GW) of battery storage projects since 2022 that can power over 27 million homes.
Among the largest battery project pipelines in Europe, this storage will complement fast-expanding wind and solar energy that today provides 22% of electricity in Turkey, up from 4.5% a decade ago.
Yet this clean energy upswing is a long way from compensating for the country's overreliance on fossil fuels.

Turkey's coal-fired electricity generation increased by roughly one-third in the last decade, and in 2024 overtook Germany and Poland, which previously had the highest coal power capacity in Europe before it began to decline.
UN climate summit opens amid worsening climate crisis
Coal undermining climate ambition
Turkey is among the few industrialized countries that has yet to commit to a phaseout date for coal — the fossil fuel with the highest planet-heating emissions.
Yet at the same time, "coal's position in the electricity market in Turkey is increasingly precarious," Efe Baysal, Turkey team lead at global environment network, 350.org, told DW.

He points to high local community opposition to coal projects on environmental grounds or due to lack of financial viability. According to German nonprofit climate campaigners, Beyond Fossil Fuels, some 97% of new coal projects have been cancelled in the last decade in Turkey, in what it calls "a global record."

"Turkey's coal project failure rate is the final nail in Europe's coal coffin," said Kasia Szeniawska of Beyond Fossil Fuels in a statement earlier this year. "Coal power is finished: it's financially risky, increases costs for billpayers, harms people's health, and sabotages climate goals."
But in June, Turkey announced plans to expand one of its largest coal plants and near double its capacity.

blocks.caption: COP31 host Turkey still relies on coal for electricity and has no plans to phase it outImage: Omer Urer/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The move underlines Turkey's "conservative energy policy" and "highly insufficient" climate goals, said Umit Sahin, head of the climate change program at the Istanbul Policy Center, a global research institute.

Turkey's current climate target allows emissions to keep rising until 2038, meaning it will struggle to meet its plans to reach net zero by 2053, notes Climate Action Tracker, a climate research think tank.
Push for electrification, energy independence

Aside from climate concerns, Turkey's high dependence on imported fossil energy makes it extremely vulnerable to volatile global oil and gas markets. The nation currently imports 95% of its natural gas, 83% of crude oil and 60% of its coal — which together make up a "lion's share” of Turkey's energy capacity, said Baysal.
It is partly this dependence that has inspired Turkey's push for greater electrification at the COP31 climate conference.
In September, the country launched the "35x35" global electrification pledge, which aims to increase electrification of world economies from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035.

The goal is for electrification to replace fossil fuels, including in transport, buildings and industry, and preferably using clean energy, though this is not mandatory —heat pumps, for example, emit fewer greenhouse gases than gas boilers, even when the electricity is generated using fossil fuels.
The pledge complements existing UN climate goals of doubling energy efficiency and tripling renewables to keep temperature rise in line with the Paris climate agreement.
Turkey's mining threatens ancient olive grove heritage
Turkey COP31 President Murat Kurum will promote the 35x35 pledge in Antalya on both climate and energy security grounds.

"[The war in the Gulf] has shown us, once again, that fossil fuels do not guarantee energy supply security," he said earlier this year at a UN climate meeting in Bonn, Germany. "Investment in alternative energy sources, in particular to support energy diversity, means stability, resilience and clean development."
But despite the rhetoric, Climate Action Tracker says that under Turkey's National Energy Plan, the COP31 host is only on track to electrify around 25% of total energy consumption by 2035.
Can renewables expansion turn the tide?
Turkey is one of numerous Mediterranean countries facing extreme climate impacts like wildfires and record heat, in addition to recent severe and deadly flooding.

blocks.caption: Torrential rainfall caused severe flash floods in Istanbul in OctoberImage: Adem Kutucu/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: As it hosts this year's climate summit, the country has a great opportunity to hasten the energy transition, said Baysal, especially since it receives nearly double the annual sunlight of Germany.
Turkey is already starting to realize some of this potential, with one analysis showing the country produces more solar module manufacturing capacity than several major European countries combined.
Solar increased from around 0.1% of total installed electricity capacity in 2014 to almost 21% at the beginning of 2026, according to Turkey's resources and energy ministry.

The COP31 host can reduce its emissions 35% by 2035 if 10 GW of solar and wind is added each interim year — as opposed to the government's target of 8 GW — noted Umit Sahin. This goal will be helped by fast-expanding battery capacity, he said.
"But if you don't phase out coal, your emissions cannot go down," he added.
Meanwhile, the COP presidency could be a "turning point" and "a very important step for Turkey," said Sahin.
If the country wants to show climate leadership, and reduce energy dependency, it will need to embrace a "progressive climate policy" that promotes a full energy transition, he added.
Serdar Vardar and Jonathan Rampley-Sturgeon contributed reporting to this article.

articles.title: At least 34 dead after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal
articles.summary: The Atlantic crossing to Spain's Canary Islands remains dangerous for migrants seeking a better life

blocks.text: At least 34 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports, citing an official source.
The Interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.
The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.
Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.

Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told AFP that all the bodies recovered so far were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.
In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.
"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.
The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.
Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.
Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.
Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.
Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.
More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.
The Canary Islands have become a major entry point into Europe for migrants and refugees making the dangerous Atlantic crossing from West Africa.

The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.

Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.
Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.
The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.
In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

articles.title: ‘A global political awakening’: how gen Z protests are sweeping the world
articles.summary:
From Serbia to Bangladesh and India to France, young people are pushing back against authoritarianism and reshaping political landscapes

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions,…

blocks.text: In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.

Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.

“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.

blocks.caption: Young people gather for a protest in Brussels, Belgium, last month. Photograph: Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga/Shutterstock

blocks.text: From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.

Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.

Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.

blocks.caption: Activists gather in Dhaka in 2024 to demand action after the deaths of students during anti-quota protests. Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters

blocks.text: The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.

Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.

blocks.caption: Serbian students cycle in Austria in 2025 during a bike ride to Strasbourg to publicise protests in their country. Photograph: Igor Pavićević/Reuters

blocks.text: Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.

Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.

“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.

blocks.caption: Tens of thousands of people march in protest against the government, rearmament, and the high cost of living in Rome last month during a national strike called by the USB trade union.  Photograph: Marco Di Gianvito/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.

That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.

blocks.caption: Young people at a rally in Belo Horizonte spell out Explode, the catchphrase of the Lula Army WhatsApp group in Brazil. Photograph: Tiago Rogero/The Guardian

blocks.text: On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.

Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.

blocks.caption: Young supporters of Zohran Mamdani cheer as he speaks after winning the Democratic mayoral primary in June 2025. Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian

blocks.text: It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.

In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A protester wearing a Batman mask holds a loudspeaker during a demonstration organised by Gen Z regelt in October 2026. Photograph: Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”

A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.

blocks.caption: Supporters of the Cockroach Janta party clash with police as they attempt to march toward India’s parliament to demand the resignation of the education minister in Delhi in July 2026. Photograph: Vipin/AP

blocks.text: Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.

It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.

blocks.caption: Police attempt to break up a protest in Paris this week. Photograph: Thibault Camus/AP

blocks.text: In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.

In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.

blocks.caption: Protesters at a demonstration in Rabat, Morocco, in September 2025 calling for reforms in the public health and education sectors. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.

The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.

Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.

blocks.caption: Students from North Carolina A&T State University and UNC Greensboro march to polling places on the first day of early voting in Greensboro, North Carolina, on 15 October 2026. Photograph: Jamarious Simmons/Black Voters Matter Fund

blocks.text: As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.

Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

articles.summary: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations Nations (ASEAN) Organizing Council on Monday urged Filipinos to respect foreign delegates expected to arrive in the country for the 49th ASEAN Summit, which…

blocks.text: Published November 9, 2026 3:56pm

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations Nations (ASEAN) Organizing Council on Monday urged Filipinos to respect foreign delegates expected to arrive in the country for the 49th ASEAN Summit, which the Philippines will host next week.

Retired Maj. Gen. Potenciano Camba, the council's deputy director general for operations, said more than 20 delegations are expected to attend the summit, including representatives from the 11 ASEAN member states.
The summit is scheduled for November 16 to 18 at the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC) in Pasay City.
The Philippines previously hosted the 48th ASEAN Summit and Related Meetings in May in Cebu.
Speaking on Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon, Camba said security measures and traffic management plans were in place to ensure the safety of delegates and the public.
He acknowledged, however, that the public would have to adjust its daily routines because of expected disruptions during the event.

“We have informed our fellow Filipinos to adjust their daily routines. The MMDA, our partner under the Committee on Security, alongside local government units, has already issued a rerouting plan,” Camba said.

He also cited Proclamation No. 1447, which declared November 16, 17 and 18 as special non-working days in the National Capital Region to help ease traffic and ensure the safety of summit participants.

Addressing groups planning to stage demonstrations during the summit, Camba acknowledged their right to assemble but appealed to them to consider holding their protests after the country's hosting duties.
“Let us hear the voices of our countrymen. The Philippine National Police is fully prepared and capable of managing these situations," Camba said.
However, it would be much better if our fellow Filipinos held their protests after the summit because it would look bad if we have demonstrations while we have visitors,” he added.
Camba likened the situation to receiving guests at home, saying Filipinos should prepare for and show respect to their visitors.
The organizing council also said it was working with the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) to address potential cyberattacks and prevent the spread of misinformation.
Camba urged the public to share only verified information and refrain from spreading fake news during the summit.
He appealed for cooperation and the spirit of bayanihan to ensure the successful hosting of the regional gathering, saying the country's reputation was at stake.

The Philippines assumed the ASEAN chairmanship from Malaysia in 2026. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is expected to formally turn over the chairmanship to Singapore, which will host the bloc's summits in 2027.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Warden: Martin Romualdez's personal staff a regular visitor
articles.summary: The personal staff of former Speaker and Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez, Arvin de Guzman, gets to stay in the New Quezon City jail only during visiting hours, Jail Warden Lourdes Pacion said…

blocks.text: Published November 9, 2026 3:56pm

The personal staff of former Speaker and Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez, Arvin de Guzman, gets to stay in the New Quezon City jail only during visiting hours, Jail Warden Lourdes Pacion said Monday.

Pacion made the clarification during the hearing on Romualdez’s whereabouts before the Sandiganbayan Third Division amid allegations of columnist Ramon Tulfo that the former speaker is able to leave the BJMP facility as he pleases in an ambulance, an allegation that Tulfo has since retracted for being false.
Romualdez, on the other hand, is in detention amid a P7.4 billion plunder charge leveled against him and three others over his alleged involvement in the flood control projects kickback scheme.
“Actually, the person allowed, he is a visitor. He is included in the visitor's list,” Pacion said.
This was different from Pacion’s earlier account where she said that he allowed Romualdez’s personal staff to stay with the lawmaker 24/7 due to Romualdez’s unstable mental health condition.
Asked by the court justices if De Guzman was allowed from 8 am to 5 pm inside the cell of Romualdez, Pacion answered yes.
“After visiting hours [of 8 am to 5 pm], he is on call 24/7,” Pacion added.
Pacion also apologized before the anti-graft court for saying that the personal staff of Romualdez is with the lawmaker 24/7.
“Sorry ‘your honor, siguro nataranta lang po ako your honor, pasensiya na po,” Pacion said.
(I am sorry. I was just flustered. I apologize.)

Romualdez’s legal counsel, Judd Roy, also confirmed before the Sandiganbayan that Romualdez’s legal team asked for the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) to allow De Guzman, a longtime staff member of Romualdez, to assist the former Speaker with his medical needs.
Roy said De Guzman had worked for Romualdez for years and was familiar with his medical requirements, including the medications he needed to take. — RSJ, GMA News

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Various events are being held nationwide to mark the anniversary of the November pogroms of 1938, in which dozens of Jewish people were killed
The opening of the Berlin Wall in 1989, which ultimately led to German reunification, is also being commemorated

The trial against eight suspected members of the militant neo-Nazi group "Saxon Separatists" is to continue in Dresden

blocks.text: This is a roundup of the stories from and about Germanyhitting the headlines on Monday, November 9, 2026:
November 9, 2026
Germany marks November pogroms anniversary

blocks.caption: Hundreds of synagogues were set on fire during the pogromsImage: akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Commemorations are to be held nationwide to commemorate the Nazi pogroms of November 9-10, 1938, when mobs went on an antisemitic rampage, killing at least 91 Jewish people, ransacking Jewish businesses and burning down hundreds of synagogues.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is to attend events in the eastern city of Weimar, where he is due to lay a wreath and hold a speech at the memorial site established at the site of the former Nazi concentration camp of Buchenwald.
The Jüdische Gemeinde zu Berlin is to have all the names of Jewish Nazi victims read out over the day in commemoration of the pogroms.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be attending a ceremony marking the 20th anniversary of the Ohel Jakob Main Synagogue in Munich, which was opened 68 years to the day after the main synagogue in the city was destroyed in the pogroms.
The pogroms are sometimes known as "Reichskristallnacht" or "Night of Broken Glass," but this name has fallen out of favor as underplaying the horrors of what happened.

articles.title: COP31 summit leaders urge world to ‘move faster’ on climate
articles.summary: The comments at the start of the two-week UN conference are an appeal to governments to focus on climate, even as other international crises from war to soaring inflation and the uncertainty of AI…

blocks.text: COP31. Vehicles drive under an overpass near the venue on the opening day of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9, 2026.
Murad Sezer/Reuters

The comments at the start of the two-week UN conference are an appeal to governments to focus on climate, even as other international crises from war to soaring inflation and the uncertainty of AI compete for their attention

items: Leaders at COP31 in Turkey emphasized the urgent need to combat climate change as global temperatures rise and climate-related disasters increase.
The summit aims to electrify over a third of the global economy by 2035, but critics argue the pledge lacks requirements for low-carbon energy sources.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ANTALYA, Turkey – Leaders of the COP31 climate summit urged the world to accelerate the fight against global warming as rising temperatures and an increasing number of climate-driven disasters threaten lives and the global economy, as the annual meeting began in Turkey on Monday, November 9.

The comments at the start of the two-week UN conference were an appeal to governments to focus on climate, even as other international crises from war to soaring inflation and the uncertainty of AI compete for their attention.

“The urgency of this moment must drive us forward,” UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said in prepared remarks for the opening of the event on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, adding that progress so far was “nowhere near fast enough.”

A report by the United Nations Environment Programme published in October said the world was already set to overshoot 1.5ºC of warming above pre-industrial times, the threshold set at the 2015 Paris climate summit to avoid the worst consequences of warming.

This year is on track to be one of the four hottest on record, driven by a powerful El Niño, a UN report showed on Monday. 2026 has also stood out with a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flood killing more than 1,450 people, with thousands still ​missing.

Turkey’s COP31 presidency has focused this year’s summit on a goal to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from around a fifth today. It is asking nations to sign onto a pledge supporting that target.

Theoretically, such a goal could help reduce planet-warming emissions by speeding the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, furnaces, boilers, cooking stoves, and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment.

“We want people to feel the results of climate talks in daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford and in new jobs,” Turkey’s COP31 President Murat Kurum said in prepared remarks.

But climate advocates have criticized the pledge because it does not require the additional electricity to come from low-carbon sources, setting up an early fight over whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.

blocks.caption: The ocean can be our best bet vs climate change. It’s finally at the heart of COP31.

blocks.text: The Iran war has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels, as has Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the ensuing sanctions on Moscow’s energy exports, though some say the wars have also shown the benefits of moving to renewables.
The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted Middle East oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting fuel prices around the globe and prompting a scramble for new supplies.

US President Donald Trump’s administration — which is shunning climate talks for the second year running — has encouraged policies maximizing oil, gas, and coal production to address the Mideast disruptions.
South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations, meanwhile, have also increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.

“A lot of people who previously might have been embarrassed to argue for continuing very high use of fossil fuel are now feeling empowered to make that case,” said John Holdren of Harvard University, who was a science adviser to Barack Obama when he was US president.
At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean tech from China, cheering advocates for ambitious climate action.
Stiell told the summit renewables were the clear answer to improving energy security.
“This year’s fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shockwave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer,” he said.
“But the solutions are clear,” he added, saying renewable energy installations had saved the global economy hundreds of billions of dollars.
The rapid rollout of AI is also complicating talks, driving a surge in global power demand and contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions.
Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions at COP31 to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s president of COP31 negotiations, said he hoped the conference would show the world that multilateralism works.
“Paris is working,” he said, referring to the landmark 2015 deal to limit global warming. “But we must move faster.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Pork import ban too little too late? Tariff hike sought to protect hog farmers
articles.summary: Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel officially announces a 60-day ban on pork imports after signing the order on Sunday, November 8

blocks.text: RALLY. Local hog raisers stage a protest at the Department of Agriculture headquarters in Quezon City on October 23, 2026, demanding that the government support the industry and control pork imports by reinstating tariff controls to help them compete in the market.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel officially announces a 60-day ban on pork imports after signing the order on Sunday, November 8

items: The Philippines has imposed a 60-day ban on pork imports to address collapsing farm gate prices, but agricultural groups argue that higher import tariffs are necessary for long-term protection of the local industry.
Hog producers are calling for the reinstatement of previous tariff rates of 40% out-quota and 30% in-quota, as current rates are seen as insufficient.
Agriculture Secretary Tiu Laurel indicated that the ban could be extended if prices do not improve, and he noted that there is currently an oversupply of pork in the market.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ recent pork import ban is too little, too late for pork producers and agricultural groups demanding reforms to alleviate a domestic industry suffering from collapsing farm gate prices.
What they want is the restoration of higher pork import tariffs which they said would ultimately protect the local industry.
Hog producers want to reinstate previous tariff rates of 40% out-quota and 30% in-quota. Current rates are at 25% and 15%, respectively.
“[The suspension] should be extended,” said Alyansa Agrikultura chairman Ernesto Ordoñez on Monday, November 9. “It is useless unless the tariffs are changed.”

Ordoñez was speaking at a press briefing held at the Department of Agriculture (DA) in Quezon City on Monday, together with other groups and Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. Last October, groups rallied in front of the DA office calling for the import ban and tariff reform.
During the presser, Tiu Laurel announced the Philippines’ imposition of a 60-day ban on pork imports, through Department Order 33 that he signed on Sunday, November 8.

The DA found that pork imports increased by 41.8% from 2023 to 2025. The gap between imports and domestic production considerably increased, causing farm gate prices to collapse and inflicting serious injury to the local industry.
For months, agricultural groups have sounded the alarm on the need for tariff protection.

“Lahat ng mga produkto na pino-produce natin dito sa ating bansa ay dapat protektahan,” said Chester Tan of the National Federation of Hog Farmers Inc. “Ito po, ano pong damage na nagawa nila? Hindi lang po sa aming mga commercial hog farmers na medium-scale, small-scale, [pati] iyon pong ating mga kasama na backyard raiser.”
(All our local produce should be protected. Who is harmed with the damage they inflicted? Not only commercial hog farmers that are medium-scale, small-scale, but backyard raisers.)
After the DA imposed this suspension – which Tiu Laurel said was already in the works since July – stakeholders called on the Tariff Commission to make the necessary changes.
The DA chief himself said the reinstatement of tariff rates to the previous 40% out-quota and 30% in-quota is the “ultimate, final solution.”

blocks.caption: PROTEST. Local hog raisers stage a protest at the Department of Agriculture Headquarters in Quezon City on October 23, 2026, demanding that the government support the industry and control pork imports by reinstating tariff controls to help them compete in the market. A 3-day pig holiday is in eff…

blocks.text: Tiu Laurel assured groups that the ban can be extended if farm gate prices do not improve.
“Huwag mag-alala sa 60 days kung kailangan i-extend ‘yan, we have until 140 days na puwedeng paglaruan at pag-aralan,” said Tiu Laurel. (We have 140 days more if we need to extend the 60-day ban.)
An increase of P50 in farm gate prices would be a good sign, according to Tiu Laurel. Current farm gate prices range from P140 to P150 per kilo.
The Philippines still has pork supply good for 170 days or almost six months, according to the DA. This Christmas season, Tiu Laurel said he does not see any unusual spikes in pork prices.
“Hindi dapat tumaas kasi nga tulad ng sinabi ng ating mga kasama or experts ngayon dito, there is an oversupply of pork products in our market,” said Tiu Laurel.
(Prices should not increase because as mentioned by our colleagues and experts present here, there is an oversupply of pork products in our market.) – Rappler.com

articles.title: Solon calls for targeted, accessible housing finance programs
articles.summary: A member of the House committee on banks and financial intermediaries has called for targeted, accessible housing finance programs for middle- and lower-income first-time buyers to cushion the impact…

blocks.text: A member of the House committee on banks and financial intermediaries has called for targeted, accessible housing finance programs for middle- and lower-income first-time buyers to cushion the impact of prolonged monetary tightening.

Rep. JP Padiernos said policymakers should explore targeted financing assistance, more accessible housing loan terms, and stronger coordination among government agencies, housing finance institutions, and private developers.

He said that measures should be designed around the actual financing capacity of prospective homebuyers, with transparent loan terms and safeguards to ensure that monthly amortizations remain manageable and sustainable.

The lawmaker made the statement amid the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ 50-basis-point interest rate hike to 5.50%, which he said could further push homeownership out of reach for Filipino families, especially as credit terms tighten amid growing risks of stagflation in the country.
“For Filipino families, the central question is whether financing and housing options will remain attainable as monetary policy stays tight to combat inflation,” Padiernos said.
“For policymakers and the property sector, the immediate challenge is maintaining financial stability without completely closing the door on affordable homeownership,” he added.

He further said that higher borrowing costs add severe pressure to an already struggling residential property market, particularly amid concerns over slowing economic growth and persistent inflation, which could further constrain household purchasing power and access to housing finance..

S&P Global Ratings recently warned of the country’s worsening macroeconomic backdrop, pointing to a sharp slowdown in first-half 2026 GDP growth to just 2.6% alongside October inflation surging to a near four-year high of 7.8%. The rating agency projects full-year 2026 GDP growth to reach a modest 2.9%, with annual inflation averaging 5.5%.

With high oil prices and a strong El Niño pattern expected to drive food costs higher, S&P expects consumer spending to weaken further and squeeze household budgets through the first half of 2027. Consequently, the central bank is anticipated to keep interest rates higher for longer to contain persistent price pressures, even if supply-side relief eventually limits additional policy rate hikes.

“For families planning to buy a house or condominium through a bank loan, the BSP’s rate decision raises serious concerns about affordability, particularly as stagflationary pressures, rising food, electricity, fuel, and transportation costs, continue to erode household purchasing power,” said Padiernos.

While the BSP’s benchmark policy rate does not automatically yield an identical, immediate increase across all commercial housing loans, the lawmaker noted that higher benchmark rates directly influence banks’ underlying lending costs and repricing schedules.

“The BSP has an important role in maintaining price stability, which is essential to protecting the purchasing power of Filipino families. At the same time, we must examine complementary measures to ensure that higher borrowing costs do not further limit access to affordable housing,” Padiernos said.
“When mortgage rates escalate precisely as basic necessities consume a larger share of disposable income, homeownership becomes vastly more difficult to achieve,” he added.

The pressure on domestic real estate demand was evident even prior to the BSP's policy tightening. Data from real estate consulting firm Colliers Philippines revealed that net take-up of Metro Manila condominiums dropped to just 500 units in the second quarter of 2026, a 60% decline from the previous quarter and the lowest quarterly performance in five quarters.

Colliers also observed a clear shift toward lower-priced inventory: condominiums priced between P1.8 million and P3.6 million accounted for 67% of total net take-up in the first half of 2026, up from 33% in the same period last year. This trend underscores a tightening constraint on buyer affordability across Metro Manila.

To navigate the high-interest, high-inflation landscape, Colliers urged property developers to re-evaluate selling strategies and structure more flexible, extended payment arrangements, particularly for residential units priced between P2.5 million and P12 million. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Davao assessor unable to verify P6-M property in Sara's SALN
articles.summary: Duterte's defense establishes location match, but P6-million property link remains unclear.

blocks.text: November 9, 2026 | 3:28pm
Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin answers questions at the Senate impeachment court on Nov. 9, 2026.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — The first defense witness in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial testified Monday, November 9 that two barangay names linked to her disputed property declarations refer to the same area in Davao City.

Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin said Barangay 74-A and Matina Crossing are the same area, potentially explaining a discrepancy in the location of properties listed in Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

But when questioned about a property purchased by Duterte's husband, Manases Carpio, for P6 million in 2024, Adalin said he could not say with certainty whether it was the same property listed in her SALN.

Duterte faces an impeachment allegation that she failed to fully disclose her assets and liabilities, including properties in Matina. While other charges against her have been dropped before the Senate impeachment court, she remains accused of unexplained wealth and discrepancies in her SALN.
During the defense's examination of Adalin, lawyer Lindon Baquel sought to establish that Barangay 74-A and Matina Crossing referred to the same location.
Benjamin Tolosa, counsel for the prosecution, said the prosecution panel was willing to stipulate that the document presented showed the two names referred to the same area.
The defense, however, preferred to have Adalin confirm this himself.
Questions over P6-M property

Tolosa later confronted Adalin with an Electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration, or eCAR, dated July 2024, which showed that Carpio purchased a property for an actual selling price of P6 million.
Asked whether he could say with 100% certainty that the property covered by the transfer certificate of title, or TCT was the same property declared in Duterte's SALN, Adalin said he was uncertain.
Adalin explained that the subpoena issued to his office had asked him to verify a specific TCT.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero also questioned Adalin about the property records.

"If this honorable impeachment court would require us to submit or subpoena to submit all properties on by Attorney Manases (Carpio) in that particular barangay, then we will submit your honor," Adalin said.
Alleged failure to disclose. Article II of the Articles of Impeachment includes allegations that Duterte failed to fully disclose her assets and liabilities, including properties in Barangay Matina.
In October, a witness from the Land Registration Authority identified a 379-square-meter lot in Matina that Carpio purchased for P6 million in 2024.
The witness testified that the property did not match any entry in Duterte's 2025 SALN based on its price, location or mode of acquisition.

articles.title: Over 19,800 cops to secure ASEAN Summit 2026
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) will deploy 19,869 police personnel to secure the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits on November 16 to 18, 2026.

blocks.text: Published November 9, 2026 3:12pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) will deploy 19,869 police personnel to secure the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits on November 16 to 18, 2026.
At a press briefing on Monday, PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said, “The PNP is ready to provide security for the heads of state, foreign delegates, and other expected guests.

He said the police personnel will “secure the summit venues, the hotels, the billeting areas, and motorcade routes in close coordination with the Armed Forces of the Philippines, the Presidential Security Command, other agencies, and the local government units.”
Nartatez said security preparations began last year and are already being implemented.
He said authorities had prepared the necessary security plans, resources, and contingencies for the international gathering.
Nartatez also said the police would be placed on heightened alert and full alert during the summit activities.
According to him, 639 meetings and activities related to the ASEAN Summit had been scheduled, with around 400 already completed and 159 still remaining.
Meanwhile, Nartatez reminded the public that November 16 to 18 had been declared special non-working days in Metro Manila.
He encouraged residents to monitor official traffic and security advisories and plan their trips accordingly. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: ‘It’s a feeling of being screwed over’: once-quiet village despairs over ‘monster’ warehouse
articles.summary:
Residents of Astley in Greater Manchester will tell public inquiry next week of ‘cacophony’ of noise causing sleep deprivation and depression

When Stephen Retford retired from the police in…
articles.byline: Josh Halliday North of England editor

blocks.text: When Stephen Retford retired from the police in 2006, he looked forward to a quiet life after nearly three decades catching villains. But now the former detective has landed another big case – one that is extremely close to home.

“It’s the total injustice of it,” the 70-year-old seethed, staring up at the 18-metre-high mega-warehouse that looms over the quiet village of Astley in Greater Manchester. Residents are up in arms about the “monster” construction, likening it to having a “cruise ship in our back garden”.

Andy Burnham expressed concern over the development weeks before he became prime minister, and Bev Craig, his successor as Greater Manchester mayor, said she too was concerned. “Old industry wouldn’t have got that close to your house,” she said. “So why is it that new industry can?”

This week, villagers will attempt to block plans by Whistl, the distribution firm that operates the warehouse, to use dozens of HGVs and trailers for its round-the-clock operation. In a two-day public inquiry, they will describe how the “cacophony” of noise is already driving some to sleep deprivation and depression.

“It’s had a profound impact on the neighbourhood,” said Retford, a burly man with a booming voice who after so many years in the police is not easily shaken. “The noise wakes you up at 2am and you can’t get back to sleep. We’ve not had a proper night’s sleep in well over a year. It’s a living hell.”

This once-quiet village is now on the frontline in a nationwide fightback against superstructures springing up everywhere from Devon to Cardiff and the Scottish Borders. Plans were announced last week for Britain’s largest datacentre at the site of the Drax power plant in North Yorkshire, and a further 315 “hyperscale” datacentres are queueing to connect to the National Grid.

Down the road from Retford’s house, a woman looked out of her daughter’s bedroom window at the Whistl warehouse just metres away. The woman, a police officer who does not want to be named, said her 10-year-old son, who is autistic, refused to play in the garden because of the “continuously whirring” noise of the conveyor belts. Her eight-year-old daughter has become too scared to play in her bedroom.

“As soon as she comes home from school, those blinds will be shut because she doesn’t want anyone to see in,” she said, pointing to a CCTV camera on the warehouse facing their home. “She hates it. She does get scared about it.”

Like many of their neighbours, the woman and her husband moved to Astley before plans had been submitted by a firm part-owned by Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners, run by the billionaire John Whittaker.

blocks.caption: Stephen Retford in his back garden: ‘We’ve not had a proper night’s sleep in well over a year.’ Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: Back then, they were surrounded by farmland where lambs, cows and horses grazed. Now their view is a giant hunk of grey steel that was named the worst new building in the UK this year. “It was a lovely view, so secluded,” she said. “When we saw the structure of this, it was like: oh my God, what is this?”

As mayor, Burnham said earlier this year that the development had not been managed properly and that key things “should have been done differently”. Wigan council said it acted properly in approving the superstructure despite objections from the local MP and dozens of residents. However, the council’s leader, Labour’s Nazia Rehman, admitted last month that “some lessons have been learned” and said that in future “consultations [with residents] will be proactive”. Local leaders have scrapped plans for four other giant warehouses in response to the backlash.

Helen Halbous, who moved to the estate seven years ago, said: “It’s a feeling of being screwed over by Wigan council, having been born and brought up here. People who had a voice of power [in the council] either made this awful decision or they looked away and let it happen. It was a little mining village and now we’re this industrial centre. It’s so wrong.”

blocks.caption: The view from Halbous’s back window. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: Halbous, 47, said she and her partner, Sami Halbous, now felt trapped in a house they once loved and they feared they would be unable to sell up. “A neighbour had their home valued and they lost 30%, and that’s if they can sell,” she said.

Residents felt hoodwinked about the size of the structure and its closeness to their homes, Halbous said. “The plan in 2019 was it was to be used for employment. It was never to have an 18-metre-high warehouse. Those permissions were changed [before 2024] and changed really quietly. We wouldn’t have bought here and let ourselves get trapped like this.”

PLP, the land owner, said the size and scale of the buildings had not changed since its planning application in 2023. It said earlier plans for smaller units, submitted in 2017 by Peel, one of its biggest shareholders, had since lapsed.

Wigan council said it recognised the “strength of feeling in the community and do not underestimate the impact residents tell us the development has had on them”. It said an independent review found its planning process was “legally sound” and followed national guidelines but there were “lessons around engagement and transparency”. It said: “We have acknowledged those findings and have taken steps to improve our approach.”

Whistl, which began operating at the site in July, has responded to the concerns by promising to use quieter vehicles and stopping their use outside between midnight and 6am. The firm said it took residents’ concerns seriously and was “committed to meeting its licensing responsibilities and being a good neighbour”. A Whistl spokesperson said the noise mitigation measures would remain in place and the overnight pause on activity in the yard would continue while all parties tried to “identify a sustainable, long-term solution”.

Retford became so fed up with the disturbance that he began overnight observations to track the big vehicles clanking around near his home. He commissioned independent acoustics experts to produce a sound report, convinced that the “cacophony of rolling thunder, a booming sound”, breached regulations.

blocks.caption: Residents have complained of a ‘cacophony’ of noise. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: A fightback fund launched by residents has so far raised £78,000, much of which will be spent on lawyers for next week’s public inquiry.

For Retford and his wife, Carole, 71, the impact has been huge. “Bloody hell, there’s not a lot of things I’ve not seen in my life,” he said. “I don’t get easily shocked and I’m not a flaky character, but this has had a profound effect on me. We’re not fuddy-duddies or nimbies. This is big business riding over the little people like us, saying ‘screw the lot of you’.”
Retford and his wife have spoken to their doctor about sleep deprivation. “It’s a torture for a very good reason, because it just drains you – and that is the effect it’s having on us,” he said.

Carole became close to tears. Staring up at the warehouse, she said: “It’s changed our lives. Your moods go up and down to being very depressed and very emotional about it because there’s no way out at the minute. People use the ‘depression’ word too lightly, but if you feel there’s no way out, it does get to you.”

articles.title: ‘Closed’ chapter: Leni Robredo not running for president in 2028
articles.summary: Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo reiterates her April statement that she will only seek reelection as mayor in 2028

blocks.text: LENI. Former vice president Leni Robredo endorses Francis 'Kiko' Pangilinan and Bam Aquino for the Senate in the 2025 national and local elections, during a kick-off rally in Dasmariñas, Cavite on February 11, 2025.
Angie de Silva/Rappler
Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo reiterates her April statement that she will only seek reelection as mayor in 2028
MANILA, Philippines – Saying she is not politically savvy enough for a national position, Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo on Monday, November 9, thumbed down a presidential bid in 2028.

In a radio interview on RMN DWNX Naga, Robredo sought to put an end to speculation about a possible 2028 bid, amid surveys showing her as the closest rival to the current top contender, Vice President Sara Duterte.
Robredo said that for her, a potential 2028 presidential run is “closed” and that nothing can change her mind.

The former vice president had said as much back in April, when she said that she would “not anymore” seek a second presidential run and that she would rather work on reelection as Naga mayor in 2028. (READ: Robredo rules out 2028 national bid, eyes Naga reelection)
Robredo was a distant second in the 2022 presidential elections with 15 million votes, against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s 31.6 million.
After her 2022 loss, she focused on her Angat Buhay Foundation before returning to politics in 2025, this time to run for Naga mayor.

In her Monday interview, Robredo, who served as vice president during the Rodrigo Duterte administration, said that she knew that she would not withstand national politics and that she was still not well-versed in dealing with politicians.

Pre-election surveys on potential 2028 presidential contenders have consistently shown Robredo as the closest rival of Duterte, who declared her intention to run for president as early as February this year.
Duterte, however, will not be able to run for public office if she gets convicted by the Senate in her ongoing impeachment trial. A decision is expected in December. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
articles.summary: At least six people were killed in the shooting and a dozen more were injured.

blocks.text: A gunman suspected of killing six people in Krakow has died in hospital, Polish police say.
The 24-year-old, who ministers said was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies", was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday.
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.
Krakow police said the suspected gunman died early on Monday morning.

After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man but did not confirm his name.

In the hours after the shooting, a minister has said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the attack.

articles.title: Leni Robredo won't run for president in 2028, will support 'deserving' candidate
articles.summary: Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo on Monday reiterated that she has no plans to run for president in the upcoming 2028 national elections.

blocks.text: Published November 9, 2026 2:42pm
Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo on Monday reiterated that she has no plans to run for president in the upcoming 2028 national elections.
Robredo, who previously served as vice president, remains among the potential presidential contenders in recent preference surveys.
However, in a media briefing in Naga City on Monday, she reaffirmed her decision to skip the May 2028 presidential race, expressing her willingness instead to support any deserving candidate.
“Ako, open ako to anyone na kaya at deserving… Pero kung ako mismo, talagang hindi na,” Robredo told reporters.
(I am open to supporting anyone who is capable and deserving... But as for myself running, it is really out of the question.)
She identified several individuals whom she views as strong candidates for the country's top post.

“Na-mention ko naman na 'yan dati. Pero among the local government officials, feeling ko matibay si Mayor Joy [Belmonte], si Mayor Vico [Sotto]... Si Senator Risa, nagsabi interesado siya,” Robredo said.
(I’ve mentioned this before, but among local government officials, I feel Mayor Joy Belmonte and Mayor Vico Sotto are strong candidates... Senator Risa has also expressed interest.)
She added that there are also potential contenders to consider from her political party, such as incumbent senator Kiko Pangilinan as well as former Liberal Party member Bam Aquino.
Robredo stressed that a presidential candidate must be capable of transcending political divides.

Reacting to political surveys where she continues to rank among presidential choices, the former vice president expressed gratitude for the public's trust, describing the support as a carryover from her 2022 campaign.
“Ako, nagpapasalamat man ako sa tiwala, pero 'yon nga rin sabi ko ang desisyon ko hali na sa mga self-assessment, ka mga kakulangan ko,” Robredo said.
(I am grateful for the trust, but as I’ve said, my decision comes from a thorough self-assessment and recognizing my own limitations.)
Reflecting on her experience in both national and local office, Robredo noted that the two roles are vastly different.

She emphasized that the country's next leader must have the strength and resolve to handle national-level challenges, especially since it requires overseeing the whole system of the government. —KG, GMA News

A gunman suspected of killing six people in Kraków has died in hospital, police in Poland…

blocks.text: A gunman suspected of killing six people in a popular market square in Kraków has died in hospital, Polish police said early on Monday.

The suspect, a 24-year-old named in local media as Michal O who authorities say was probably inspired by far-right ideologies, had been wounded in a shootout with police and had been in critical condition in hospital.
“We would like to inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died in hospital early this morning,” Malopolska Policja wrote on X.

Polish prosecutors had opened a terrorism investigation after the man opened fire on Saturday afternoon, killing six including a Briton and injuring 17, in an attack that shocked a country that was considered safer than many of its European neighbours.

Karolina Galecka, an ⁠interior ministry spokeswoman, told radio TOK FM ​on ​Monday: “There ​were many different emblems on the perpetrator’s clothing that have been partially examined and interpreted.
“These patches were ​associated with various motifs that ​are currently ‌being analysed ​by ​specialists,” she added, declining to comment further as the investigation was ongoing.
Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home after the attack were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.
Five of the wounded are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police ⁠officers were also among the injured, one of whom was in a serious condition.

As two days of national mourning began, the national prosecutor’s office said on social media it had launched an investigation into “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

The rare mass shooting has deepened concern about extremism in Poland after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.
The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

The Kraków suspect drove into the city’s main square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, at top speed at about 3pm on Saturday. Wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, he started shooting at random as he took what the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło described as a “wild ride” around the square.
